lessons.title: Lesson 1: Automations and AI agents: what is the difference?
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain the difference between a fixed automation and an AI agent, and when each fits.
This lesson builds toward: Given a business task, you will explain whether a fixed automation or an AI step fits it, and which parts stay with a person, keeping money, customer messages and record changes with a person.
An automation follows fixed rules you set: "When a new form is submitted, add a row to my sheet and email me." It does the same thing every time. It is predictable and easy to check.
An AI agent is an AI system that can decide some of its own steps to reach a goal, like reading an inquiry, deciding what kind it is, drafting a reply and choosing which tool to use next. Agents are more flexible but less predictable, and they can make mistakes confidently.
For a small business, start with fixed automations, and add AI to one step where judgment with words helps, like drafting a reply or sorting messages. Keep people in charge of anything that spends money, sends messages to customers or changes records.
Words to know:
- Automation: a set of fixed steps a computer does by itself when something happens.
- AI agent: an AI system that can choose some of its own steps to reach a goal.
- Workflow: the series of steps that gets a task done.
Try it now: Write down two repeat tasks in your business. For each, write whether a fixed automation could do it, or whether it needs judgment (a possible AI step).
You can now explain the difference between an automation and an AI agent and choose the safer fit.

check.q: What is a weakness of AI agents compared with fixed automations?
options: They are less predictable and can make mistakes confidently
check.why: Agents are more flexible but less predictable, and can be confidently wrong.

check.q: You want AI to reply to inquiries and pay supplier invoices on its own. What should you do?
options: Let the AI agent do both
Let AI draft replies, and keep paying and sending with a person
Let AI pay but not reply
check.why: Keep people in charge of spending money and sending messages to customers.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Mapping a repeat task step by step
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Break one repeat task into a clear step map.
This lesson builds toward: Given one task you repeat often, you will write a step map and mark each step as Rule, Words, Decision or Money or sending, with every step you do today included.
You cannot automate what you have not written down. Pick one task you do often and write every step as you do it today. Example for a cleaning service: (1) inquiry arrives by web form, (2) I copy name, address and job type into my sheet, (3) I write a reply with my price range, (4) I add a reminder to call back, (5) I send the quote.
Mark each step: Rule (always the same), Words (needs writing or judgment), Decision (needs the owner), Money or sending (needs approval).
Steps marked Rule can be automated. Words steps can get an AI draft. Decision and Money or sending steps stay with a person.
Step by step:
- Pick a task you do at least weekly.
- Write every step as you do it now.
- Mark each: Rule, Words, Decision, Money or sending.
- Circle the Rule steps to automate first.
Words to know:
- Step map: a numbered list of every step in a task.
- Manual: done by a person by hand.
Try it now: Write the step map for one repeat task in your business and mark every step Rule, Words, Decision or Money/sending.
You can now break a repeat task into a step map that shows what can be automated.

check.q: Which steps stay with a person?
options: Decision and Money or sending steps
check.why: Decision and Money or sending steps stay with a person; Rule steps can be automated.

check.q: You want to automate how you handle new inquiries. What do you do first?
options: Ask AI to guess your process
Write down every step as you do it today
check.why: You cannot automate what you have not written down.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Designing the workflow: trigger, actions, approval
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Design a workflow with a trigger, actions and a human approval step.
This lesson builds toward: Given your step map, you will design a workflow with a trigger, actions and a human approval step, drawn on paper, with approval placed before anything leaves the business.
Every automation has a trigger (the event that starts it) and actions (what happens next). Trigger: "new form submission". Actions: "add a row to the sheet", "draft a reply with AI", "send the draft to me for approval", "create a calendar reminder".
Put the human approval before anything leaves the business: messages to customers, payments, price changes, deleting records. The automation can prepare everything; you press send.
Draw it as boxes and arrows on paper first. Name the tool for each box: your form tool, Google Sheets or Excel, an AI step, your email, your calendar. Check that each tool connects to the connector service you plan to use.
Step by step:
- Write the trigger.
- List the actions in order.
- Insert an approval step before anything is sent or paid.
- Draw it as boxes and arrows.
- Name the tool for each box and check it connects.
Words to know:
- Trigger: the event that starts an automation.
- Action: a step the automation does after the trigger.
- Approval step: a point where a person must say yes before the workflow continues.
Try it now: Draw the workflow for your task from Lesson 2: trigger, actions, and an approval step. Write the tool name in each box.
You can now design a workflow with a trigger, actions and a human approval step.

check.why: The trigger starts the automation; the actions are what happens next.

check.q: Your design has the AI step email customers directly. What do you change?
options: Send the draft to you for approval before it goes to the customer
Add a second AI step to check the first
check.why: Human approval goes before anything leaves the business.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Building, testing and running it safely

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building it with a no-code tool
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build your workflow in a no-code automation tool.
This lesson builds toward: Using a no-code automation tool, you will build the workflow, connect your accounts and map the fields, with the AI step getting only the fields it needs and sending its draft to you.
No-code tools let you build automations by choosing from menus instead of writing code. Common ones are Zapier, Make and Microsoft Power Automate. Some apps you already use, like your form, booking or email tool, have simple automations built in. Check each tool's site for its free plan and limits.
The pattern is the same everywhere: create a new automation, choose the app and event for the trigger, sign in to connect your account, then add each action and map the fields (for example, the form's "Name" goes into the sheet's "Name" column).
For an AI step, many tools offer an action that sends text to an AI model and returns a draft. Tell it exactly what to write and give it only the fields it needs. Send the draft to yourself, not straight to the customer.
Step by step:
- Create a new automation in your chosen tool.
- Choose the trigger app and event; connect your account.
- Add each action and map the fields.
- Add the AI draft step with clear instructions and only needed fields.
- Send the draft to yourself for approval.
Words to know:
- No-code: building software by choosing options instead of writing code.
- Field mapping: telling the tool which piece of information goes where.
- Connect an account: letting the automation tool use one of your apps, after you sign in.
Try it now: Build your workflow in a no-code tool's free plan (or on paper if you cannot sign up yet): trigger, field mapping for each action, and an AI draft sent to you.
You can now build a trigger-and-action workflow in a no-code automation tool.

check.q: What does a no-code tool let you do?
options: Build automations by choosing from menus
Skip signing in to your apps
check.why: No-code tools let you build automations from menus instead of writing code.

check.q: The form has 12 fields but the AI only needs the name and job type to draft a reply. What do you send it?
options: Only the name and job type
check.why: Give the AI step only the fields it needs.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Testing with sample data and fixing what breaks
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Test the automation with sample entries and fix errors before going live.
This lesson builds toward: Given three made-up sample entries, you will test the automation and fix what breaks, one change at a time, until a normal entry, a missing-field entry and an odd-text entry all pass.
Never test on real customers. Make three sample entries with made-up names like "Test Customer" and a test email you own. Include one normal entry, one with a missing field, and one with odd text (very long, another language, emojis).
Run each and check every step: did the row land in the right columns? Did the AI draft make sense and stay on topic? Did the approval reach you? Did anything get sent that should not have?
Fix one thing at a time and test again. Common problems: wrong field mapping, a step that fails when a field is blank, an AI draft that invents prices. Fix the instructions ("Use only the price range in the field; do not invent prices") and retest.
Step by step:
- Make three sample entries: normal, missing field, odd text.
- Run each through the automation.
- Check every step's result.
- Fix one problem at a time and retest.
- Go live only when all three pass.
Words to know:
- Sample data: made-up information used for testing.
- Edge case: an unusual input that might break a process, like a blank field.
- Go live: turn the automation on for real use.
Try it now: Run three sample entries through your automation (or walk them through your paper design). Write what happened at each step and one fix.
You can now test an automation safely and fix problems before it touches real customers.

check.q: Which is an example of an odd-text sample entry?
options: A very long message with emojis
check.why: The odd-text entry has very long text, another language or emojis.

check.q: A test fails when the phone field is blank. What do you do?
options: Fix that one step and test again
check.why: Fix one thing at a time and retest.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Running it safely: logs, monitoring and an off switch
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a log, a weekly check and a way to turn the automation off.
This lesson builds toward: Once the automation is live, you will set up a log, a weekly check and a one-page description that says how to turn it off, so someone else could understand or stop it.
Once it is live, keep watching. Most tools show a history of each run; check it weekly for errors. You can also add a log row to a sheet: date, what triggered it, what it did, approved by whom.
Write a one-page description: what the automation does, its trigger and actions, which accounts it uses, who approves, and how to turn it off. Store it where a family member or staff member could find it.
Protect access: use two-step sign-in on the automation tool and connected accounts, give it access only to what it needs, keep customer card numbers and passwords out of AI steps, and remove access when a staff member leaves.
Step by step:
- Check the run history weekly.
- Add a log row for each run.
- Write the one-page description with the off switch.
- Turn on two-step sign-in and limit access.
- Review whether it still saves time every month.
Words to know:
- Run history: a list the tool keeps of every time the automation ran.
- Log: a record of what happened and when.
- Off switch: the way to turn an automation off quickly.
Try it now: Final task: finish your automation: step map, workflow with approval, three passing tests, a log and weekly check, and a one-page description with the off switch.
You can now run a business automation safely with approval, testing, logs and an off switch.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Step map Steps are missing or not marked. Every step of the task is listed and marked Rule, Words, Decision or Money or sending. Notes how long each step takes today. Workflow design No approval step, or something is sent or paid without a person. Trigger, actions and a human approval before anything leaves the business. Each box names its tool and the connections are checked. Working build The automation does not run or fields land in the wrong places. Runs from the trigger, maps fields correctly, and sends the AI draft to you. The AI step gets only the fields it needs and has clear instructions. Tested and fixed Tested on real customer data or with fewer than three entries. Normal, missing-field and odd-text sample entries all pass after fixes. Lists each problem found and the one change that fixed it. Safe running No log, weekly check or way to turn it off. Log, weekly check and a one-page description with the off switch. Two-step sign-in on and access limited to what it needs. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What goes in a log row in this lesson?
options: Date, trigger, what it did and who approved
check.why: A log row records date, trigger, what it did and who approved it.

check.q: A staff member who helped approve drafts leaves the business. What do you do?
options: Share your password with the new person
Remove their access to the automation and connected accounts
check.why: Remove access when a staff member leaves.
